items.title: Get It? (Lesson 3, p. 102): A 2.5-kg book is dropped. Why is Earth's acceleration toward the book too small to notice? Estimate it (𝑚Earth = 6.0 × 1024 kg).

body.html: The book and Earth exert equal-magnitude forces on each other (Newton's third law), but 𝑎= 𝐹/ 𝑚.
The force on each is the book's weight:

answer.html: The force on Earth equals the force on the book, but Earth's mass is so huge that 𝑎= 𝐹/ 𝑚 is only about 4.1 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>24</sup> m/s<sup>2</sup>, which is negligible.

check.html: The book's own acceleration is 𝐹/ 𝑚= 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>, which is larger by the mass ratio, about 2.4 × 10<sup>24</sup>.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 28: A weightlifter raises a barbell off the floor, with the barbell speeding up as it rises. Draw a free-body diagram for the barbell and identify the interaction pair for each force on it.

body.html: Every force has an interaction partner that acts on a different object, with equal size and opposite direction. The barbell accelerates upward, so the upward force on it is larger than gravity.
Forces ON the barbell Agent Direction Partner force exerted BY the barbell Acts on 𝐹<sup>hands</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bar</sup> lifter's hands up (larger)
the hands, directed down 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bar</sup> (weight) Earth's mass down
Earth, directed up

answer.html: Forces on the barbell: the hands' upward push (greater in size) and Earth's downward gravitational force. Forces the barbell exerts: a downward push on the hands and an upward gravitational pull on Earth's mass.

check.html: Both pairs have equal magnitudes; the hands' push exceeds the barbell's weight because the bar accelerates upward.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 29: A 3.2-kg flowerpot falls from a windowsill. Ignoring air resistance, identify the force on the pot, the force the pot exerts, and their size.

body.html: With air resistance ignored, the only force on the pot is gravity.

answer.html: Force on the pot: 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>pot</sup> = 31 N, down. Force the pot exerts: 𝐹<sup>pot</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>Earth</sup> = 31 N, an upward gravitational pull of equal size acting on Earth. Earth's resulting acceleration is negligible.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 30: A 12-kg toolbox rests on a 25-kg workbench, and the bench rests on the floor. Everything is at rest. Draw a free-body diagram for the toolbox and for the bench, find the size of each force, and identify the interaction pair between the two objects.

question.html: Each object is in equilibrium (𝑎= 0). Take 𝑔= 9.8 N/kg.

body.html: Toolbox (system 1): 𝐹<sup>bench</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>toolbox</sup> (up, the normal force) and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>toolbox</sup> (down), equal in size: (12 kg)(9.8 N/kg) = 118 N. Bench (system 2): 𝐹<sup>floor</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bench</sup> (up), 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bench</sup> = (25 kg)(9.8 N/kg) = 245 N (down), and 𝐹<sup>toolbox</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bench</sup> = 118 N (down). The upward force from the floor equals the sum of the other two:

body.alt: 𝐹floor on bench = 245 N + 118 N = 363 N

body.html: The interaction pair between the two objects is 𝐹<sup>bench</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>toolbox</sup> (acts on the toolbox) and 𝐹<sup>toolbox</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bench</sup> (acts on the bench); they are equal in magnitude (118 N) and opposite in direction.

answer.html: Two diagrams as above. Toolbox: 118 N up and 118 N down. Bench: 363 N up, 245 N down and 118 N down. The interaction pair is 𝐹<sup>bench</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>toolbox</sup> = −𝐹<sup>toolbox</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bench</sup> (118 N each). (Other pairs: 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>toolbox</sup> with 𝐹<sup>toolbox</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>Earth</sup>, and 𝐹<sup>floor</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bench</sup> with 𝐹<sup>bench</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>floor</sup>, which act on Earth and the floor, not on these two systems.)

check.html: The bench's upward arrow is the longest, since the floor supports both the bench and the toolbox ( (12 + 25) kg × 9.8 = 363 N).

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 31 (Challenge): A boy throws a 0.35-kg stone straight up. After the stone leaves his hand and is on its way up, draw the free-body diagram for the stone, and give the interaction partner of each force on it.

body.html: Once the stone has left the hand there is no contact force, and air resistance is negligible, so only the gravitational force of Earth acts on it. The stone is still moving upward but slowing, since the (downward) acceleration is opposite to its velocity.

body.alt: 𝐹Earth on stone = 𝑚𝑔= (0.35 kg)(9.8 N/kg) = 3.4 N

body.html: Free-body diagram: a single downward arrow, 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>stone</sup> = 3.4 N. The stone exerts 𝐹<sup>stone</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup> = 3.4 N, upward, on Earth.

answer.html: The only force on the stone is gravity (3.4 N, downward). The stone exerts an equal, upward gravitational force (3.4 N) on Earth's mass.

check.html: 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚= 3.43 / 0.35 = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> downward, which agrees with the slowing upward motion.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 32: Rin pulls with 47 N and Omar pulls with 38 N, both in the same direction, on a rope tied to a heavy box on the floor. They just barely get the box moving. What is the size of the friction force that the floor exerts on the box? What force does the box exert on the floor?

body.html: 𝐹<sub>Rin</sub> = 47 N, 𝐹<sub>Omar</sub> = 38 N, same direction. Unknown: the friction force of the floor on the box.

"Just barely" means the net force is about zero at that moment (𝑎≈0), so the friction force has the same size as their combined pull (Newton's second law). The box pushes back on the floor with an equal and opposite force (Newton's third law).

body.alt: 𝐹floor on box = 𝐹Rin + 𝐹Omar = 47 N + 38 N = 85 N

answer.html: 85 N (the floor's friction on the box opposes the pull; the box exerts 85 N on the floor in the opposite direction).

check.html: The box is on the verge of moving, so the forces balance.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 33 (Challenge): A cable can supply a maximum tension of 230 N. What is the greatest upward acceleration it can give an 18.5-kg load?

body.html: 𝑚= 18.5 kg, 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub><sub>, max</sub> = 230 N. Unknown: 𝑎<sub>max</sub> (upward).
Take up as positive: 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub>−𝑚𝑔= 𝑚𝑎, so 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub>/ 𝑚−𝑔.

answer.html: 𝑎<sub>max</sub> = 2.6 m/s<sup>2</sup> upward.

check.html: The load's weight is 18.5 × 9.8 = 181 N, leaving 49 N for acceleration: 49 / 18.5 ≈2.6.

items.title: Lesson 3 Check Your Progress, Problem 36: Block 1 hangs from the ceiling by rope 1; block 2 hangs from block 1 by rope 2. Both blocks have 𝑚= 3.5 kg and are at rest. Find the tension in each rope.

body.html: The tension in a massless rope equals the weight of everything hanging below it.

answer.html: The tension in the rope between the two blocks is 34 N; the tension in the rope from the ceiling is 69 N (it supports both blocks).

check.html: The upper rope carries twice the load of the lower one.

items.title: Lesson 3 Check Your Progress, Problem 37: A 2.4-kg block hangs from the lower rope of an upper block, which hangs from the ceiling. The top rope's tension is 52.0 N. Find the tension in the bottom rope and the mass of the top block.

body.html: In equilibrium, the top rope supports both blocks and the lower rope supports only the 2.4-kg block.
𝑇<sub>top</sub> = (𝑚<sub>1</sub> + 𝑚<sub>2</sub>)𝑔

answer.html: The bottom rope's tension is 24 N and the top block has a mass of 2.9 kg.

check.html: The total mass is 5.3 kg, and 5.31 × 9.8 = 52 N.

items.title: Lesson 3 Check Your Progress, Problem 38 (Critical Thinking): A dog on a leash pulls with a steady 180 N force, and the other end of the leash is tied to a fence post. The dog does not move. What is the tension in the leash? What would it be if the leash were instead held by a second dog that also pulls with 180 N the other way?

body.html: The leash is not accelerating, so the net force on it is zero. The fence post replaces the second dog: it pulls back with the same force that the dog applies (Newton's second and third laws).

Imagine cutting the leash at any point. The dog pulls one end with 180 N; the post must pull the other end with 180 N for the leash to stay at rest. The tension is the pull that each part of the leash exerts on the next, which is 180 N, not 360 N. With a second dog pulling 180 N the other way, each end is pulled by 180 N, so the tension is again 180 N.

answer.html: The tension is 180 N in both cases, because the post exerts a 180 N force back on the leash, exactly as a second dog of equal strength would.

items.title: Figure 17 and 18 questions: In a tug of war, each team pulls with 640 N on the rope and nothing moves. What is the tension in the rope? A 25-kg bucket hangs at rest from a rope; what is the tension in that rope?

question.html: The tension in the tug-of-war rope equals the pull exerted at each end. For the hanging bucket, the rope must balance the bucket's weight, since the bucket is at rest.

answer.html: Tug of war: tension = 640 N (not 1280 N). Hanging bucket: tension = 2.5 × 10<sup>2</sup> N (245 N), equal to the bucket's weight.

check.html: In both cases the rope is in equilibrium, so the tension equals the force pulling on one end.

items.title: Develop a Model to Illustrate: A 150-kg block of ice rests on a frozen lake. A steady wind pushes it east with 480 N and it begins to slide. The lake surface exerts a 350 N friction force. Draw a free-body diagram of the block and find its acceleration.

body.html: Choose the block as the system. It is in contact with the lake surface and the air; Earth's gravity is a field force. The block moves, so it accelerates in the direction of the net force. Use 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚.

Take east as +𝑥. Forces on the block: 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>block</sup> (weight), downward: (150 kg)(9.8 N/kg) = 1470 N. 𝐹<sup>lake</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>block</sup> (normal force), upward, 1470 N (no vertical acceleration). 𝐹<sup>wind</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>block</sup>, horizontal, 480 N east. 𝐹<sup>ice</sup><sup> </sup><sup>friction</sup>, horizontal, 350 N west.

answer.html: System = block. FBD: weight down and normal force up (equal lengths, 1470 N each), a 480 N arrow east for the wind, and a shorter 350 N arrow west for friction. 𝐹<sub>net</sub> = 130 N east, so 𝑎= 0.87 m/s<sup>2</sup> east.

check.html: The wind push must exceed friction for the block to start sliding; here it does, by 130 N.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon and CER: How does a large cargo parachute let a heavy crate land safely? Use this evidence: (1) a 300-kg crate falling without a parachute reaches about 55 m/s; (2) with an 8-m-diameter parachute it falls at about 6 m/s; (3) a basketball falls at about 20 m/s and a foam ball of the same size at about 8 m/s. Write a claim, evidence, and reasoning.

body.html: A large parachute greatly increases the drag force on the crate, so the crate falls at a much lower terminal velocity and lands more gently.

(1) 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= 𝑚𝑔 pulls the crate down and the drag force from the air opposes its motion. (2) The same crate reaches about 55 m/s without a parachute but only about 6 m/s with one, so the larger area changed the terminal speed. (3) At the same size, the lighter foam ball reaches a lower speed (8 m/s) than the heavier basketball (20 m/s), showing that terminal speed depends on weight and on area. (4) A falling object stops accelerating, reaching terminal velocity, when drag equals weight (𝐹<sub>net</sub> = 0 by Newton's second law).

The crate accelerates downward until drag equals weight. A parachute has a much larger surface area, so the same drag force (equal to the crate's weight) is reached at a lower speed. Because the net force is zero at terminal velocity, the velocity stays constant (Newton's first law), at the gentle 6 m/s.

answer.html: The evidence supports the claim: more drag from a larger surface area means drag equals weight at a smaller speed, so the parachute lowers the terminal velocity and lets the crate land safely.

items.title: Go Further, Data Analysis Lab: A small model rocket carries a 0.200-kg payload resting on a scale. The rocket is launched straight up. Study three stages: (a) the engine is firing and the rocket speeds up at 15 m/s² upward; (b) the engine has shut off and the rocket coasts upward, with no parachute and negligible air drag; (c) the parachute is fully open and the rocket descends at constant velocity. Up is positive. Problem 1: free-body diagrams

question.html: Draw a free-body diagram of the rocket for each stage.

(a) Engine firing: the thrust force on the rocket (upward) is greater than the weight (downward), so 𝐹<sub>net</sub> and 𝑎 point up. (b) Engine off, coasting, no parachute: only the weight 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>rocket</sup> acts (air drag is neglected); the net force and acceleration are downward and equal to 𝑔. (The rocket is still moving upward and slowing down.) (c) Parachute open, descending at constant velocity: the net force is zero, so the drag force on the rocket (upward) equals the weight (downward).

answer.html: (a) thrust up (long) and weight down (shorter); (b) weight only, down; (c) drag up and weight down, equal in length.

stepCards.label: Givens
stepCards.html: Stages: (a) a = +15 m/s<sup>2</sup>, (b) engine off, (c) constant v.

stepCards.label: Equation
stepCards.html: Fnet = ma.

stepCards.label: Substitute
stepCards.html: Compare the up and down forces in each stage: net up, net down, then zero.

stepCards.label: Answer
stepCards.html: (a) thrust up (long) and weight down (shorter); (b) weight only, down; (c) drag up and weight down, equal in length.

items.title: 2: scale reading compared with the reading at rest

body.html: With up positive, the scale reading is 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> = 𝑚(𝑔+ 𝑎), which is compared with 𝑚𝑔. At rest: 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> = 𝑚𝑔= (0.200 kg)(9.8 N/kg) = 1.96 N. (a) Engine firing: 𝑎= + 15 m/s<sup>2</sup>, so
(b) Engine off, coasting: the payload, scale, and rocket all accelerate at 𝑎= −𝑔, so 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> = 𝑚(𝑔−𝑔) = 0. (c) Parachute open, constant velocity: 𝑎= 0, so 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> = 𝑚𝑔= 1.96 N.

answer.html: (a) greater than at rest (4.96 N versus 1.96 N); (b) less than at rest (zero, apparent weightlessness); (c) equal to the reading at rest (1.96 N).

items.title: 3: evidence and reasoning

answer.html: Newton's second law ties the net force to the acceleration: 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> −𝑚𝑔= 𝑚𝑎. While the engine fires, the net force on the payload is upward, so the scale must push up harder than the weight, and the reading is larger (4.96 N). Once the engine shuts off, the weight is the only force on the rocket and the scale, so everything accelerates together at 𝑔; the scale has nothing to push back against and reads zero (the real weight 𝑚𝑔 has not changed, but the apparent weight is zero). With the parachute open and the velocity constant, the net force is zero (𝑎= 0), so the scale reads the same as at rest.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 3, p. 102): why Earth's acceleration is so small

body.html: The ball and Earth exert equal-magnitude forces on each other (Newton's third law), but 𝑎= 𝐹/ 𝑚.

The same force acts on both, so the acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass. Earth's mass (6.0 × 10<sup>24</sup> kg) is enormous compared with the mass of any ordinary object, so Earth's acceleration is tiny (for a 0.18 kg ball it is about 3 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>25</sup> m/s<sup>2</sup>).

answer.html: The force on Earth equals the force on the object, but Earth's mass is so huge that 𝑎= 𝐹/ 𝑚 is negligibly small.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 30: suitcase on a luggage cart (Figure 16)

question.html: The cart is stationary, so each object is in equilibrium (𝑎= 0). The figure shows a suitcase standing on a cart with wheels on the floor.

body.html: Suitcase (system 1): 𝐹<sup>cart</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>suitcase</sup> (up, the normal force) and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>suitcase</sup> (down), equal in size. Cart (system 2): 𝐹<sup>floor</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>cart</sup> (up), 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>cart</sup> (down), and 𝐹<sup>suitcase</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>cart</sup> (down). items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 31 (Challenge): ball tossed up, after leaving the hand

body.html: Once the ball has left the hand there is no contact force, and air resistance is negligible, so only the gravitational force of Earth acts on it. The ball is still moving upward but slowing, since the (downward) acceleration is opposite to its velocity.

Free-body diagram: a single downward arrow, 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>. The ball exerts 𝐹<sup>ball</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup>, an upward gravitational force of equal size, on Earth.

answer.html: The only force on the ball is gravity (𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>, downward). The ball exerts an equal, upward gravitational force on Earth's mass.

check.html: Net force down equals 𝑚𝑔, so 𝑎= 𝑔 downward, which agrees with the slowing upward motion.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 32: Diego and Mika and the tire

body.html: 𝐹<sub>Mika</sub> = 23 N, 𝐹<sub>Diego</sub> = 31 N, same direction. They "just barely" move the tire. Unknown: the magnitude of the force between tire and wheel.
"Just barely" means the net force is about zero at that moment (𝑎≈0), so the force holding the tire on the wheel has the same size as their combined pull (Newton's second and third laws).

body.alt: 𝐹wheel on tire = 𝐹Mika + 𝐹Diego = 23 N + 31 N = 54 N

answer.html: 54 N (the wheel holds on to the tire with 54 N, and the tire pulls back on the wheel with 54 N).

check.html: The tire is on the verge of moving, so the forces balance.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 33 (Challenge): greatest acceleration of the bucket

body.html: 𝑚= 42 kg, 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub><sub>, max</sub> = 450 N. Unknown: 𝑎<sub>max</sub> (upward).
Take up as positive: 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub>−𝑚𝑔= 𝑚𝑎, so 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub>/ 𝑚−𝑔.

answer.html: 𝑎<sub>max</sub> = 0.91 m/s<sup>2</sup> upward.

check.html: The bucket's weight is 42 × 9.8 = 412 N, only 38 N below the 450 N limit, so very little acceleration is allowed (38 / 42 ≈0.9).

question.html: Block 1 hangs from the ceiling by rope 1; block 2 hangs from block 1 by rope 2. Both blocks have 𝑚= 5.0 kg and are at rest.

body.html: The tension in a massless rope equals the weight of everything hanging below it.

answer.html: The tension in the rope between the two blocks is 49 N; the tension in the rope from the ceiling is 98 N (it supports both blocks).

check.html: The upper rope carries twice the load of the lower one.

𝑇<sub>top</sub> = (𝑚<sub>1</sub> + 𝑚<sub>2</sub>)𝑔

answer.html: The bottom rope's tension is 29 N and the top block has a mass of 3.4 kg.

items.title: Lesson 3 Check Your Progress, Problem 38 (Critical Thinking): tug of war with a tree

body.html: The rope is not accelerating, so the net force on it is zero. The tree replaces the other team: it pulls back with the same force that the pulling team applies (Newton's second and third laws).

Cut the rope in thought into two pieces at any point. The team pulls one end with 500 N; the tree must pull the other end with 500 N for the rope to stay at rest. The tension is the pull that each part of the rope exerts on the next, which is 500 N, not 1000 N.

answer.html: The tension is 500 N, exactly the same as when a second team of equal strength pulled the other end, because the tree exerts a 500 N force back on the rope.

items.title: Develop a Model to Illustrate: free-body diagram of a sliding rock

body.html: Choose the rock as the system and draw a circle around it in the sketch. The rock is in contact with the ground (mud), the thin ice sheet, and the air; the Earth's gravity is a field force. The rock starts to move, so it accelerates in the direction of the net force.

Take the direction of the ice sheet's push as +𝑥. Forces on the rock: 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>rock</sup> (weight), downward. 𝐹<sup>ground</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>rock</sup> (normal force), upward, equal to the weight (no vertical acceleration). 𝐹<sup>ice</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sheet</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>rock</sup> (wind-driven push), horizontal, in the direction of motion. 𝐹<sup>mud</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>rock</sup> (friction), horizontal, opposite to the motion.
The rock only begins to slide if the push from the ice exceeds friction, so the net force (and the acceleration) points in the direction of the push.

answer.html: System = rock (circled in the sketch). FBD: weight down, normal force up (equal lengths), a long horizontal arrow for the ice sheet's push in the direction of motion, and a shorter horizontal arrow for friction opposite to it. 𝐹<sub>net</sub> and 𝑎 point in the direction of motion.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon and CER: how do wingsuits help BASE jumpers control their velocity?

body.html: A wingsuit increases the drag force on the jumper, so the jumper falls at a lower terminal velocity (and can adjust it by changing body shape).

(1) 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= 𝑚𝑔 pulls the jumper down and the drag force from the air opposes the motion. (2) Drag increases with speed and with the surface area and shape of the object. (3) A falling object stops accelerating, reaching terminal velocity, when drag equals weight (𝐹<sub>net</sub> = 0 by Newton's second law). (4) Data from the book: a spread-eagle skydiver reaches about 60 m/s, but with a parachute (very large area) about 5 m/s; a table-tennis ball (large area for its weight) reaches 9 m/s, a baseball 42 m/s.

The jumper accelerates downward until drag equals weight. A wingsuit has a much larger surface area, so the same drag force is reached at a lower speed, and the jumper changes drag (and so speed) by changing posture. Because the net force is zero at terminal velocity, the velocity stays constant (Newton's first law).

answer.html: The evidence supports the claim: more drag from a larger surface area means drag equals weight at a smaller speed, so wingsuits lower the terminal velocity and give the jumper control over velocity.

items.title: 1: free-body diagrams

question.html: (a) Engine firing: the thrust force on the rocket (upward) is greater than the weight (downward), so 𝐹<sub>net</sub> and 𝑎 point up. (b) Engine off, parachute not yet deployed: only the weight 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>rocket</sup> acts (air drag is small and is neglected); the net force and acceleration are downward and equal to 𝑔. (The rocket may still be moving upward and slowing down.) (c) The moment the parachute is deployed (at the maximum height): the rocket's velocity is momentarily zero, and the drag force depends on velocity, so at that instant the drag is zero and only the weight acts. An instant later, as the rocket begins to fall, a small upward drag force appears and grows with speed until it equals the weight (terminal velocity).

answer.html: (a) thrust up (long) and weight down (shorter); (b) weight only, down; (c) weight down, and drag upward that is zero at the very top and grows as the rocket speeds up while falling.

stepCards.label: Givens
stepCards.html: Stages: (a) engine firing, (b) engine off, (c) parachute opens at the top.

stepCards.label: Equation
stepCards.html: Fnet = ma; drag depends on v.

stepCards.label: Substitute
stepCards.html: Compare forces in each stage; at the top v = 0 m/s, so drag starts at 0 N.

stepCards.label: Answer
stepCards.html: (a) thrust up (long) and weight down (shorter); (b) weight only, down; (c) weight down, and drag upward that is zero at the very top and grows as the rocket speeds up while falling.

items.title: 2: scale reading compared with the reading at rest

body.html: With up positive, the scale reading is 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> = 𝑚(𝑔+ 𝑎), which is compared with 𝑚𝑔. (a) Engine firing: 𝑎> 0 (upward), so 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> > 𝑚𝑔. (b) Engine off, before the parachute: the person, scale, and rocket all accelerate at 𝑎= −𝑔, so 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> = 𝑚(𝑔−𝑔) = 0. (c) The moment the parachute deploys: the drag is still zero at that instant (𝑣= 0), so the rocket still accelerates at −𝑔 and 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> ≈0 (it then rises from zero as drag builds, and returns to 𝑚𝑔 at terminal velocity).

answer.html: (a) greater than at rest; (b) less than at rest (about zero, apparent weightlessness); (c) less than at rest (about zero at that instant).

stepCards.label: Givens
stepCards.html: Up positive; a > 0, then a = -g, then a = -g at deployment.

stepCards.label: Equation
stepCards.html: Fscale = m(g + a).

stepCards.label: Substitute
stepCards.html: (a) m(g + a) > mg; (b) m(g - g) = 0 N; (c) m(g - g) = 0 N.

stepCards.label: Answer
stepCards.html: (a) greater than at rest; (b) less than at rest (about zero, apparent weightlessness); (c) less than at rest (about zero at that instant).

items.title: 3: evidence and reasoning

answer.html: Newton's second law ties the net force to the acceleration: 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> −𝑚𝑔= 𝑚𝑎. While the engine fires, the net force on the person is upward, so the scale must push up harder than the weight, and the reading is larger. Once the engine shuts off, the weight is the only force on the rocket and the scale, so everything falls together with 𝑎= 𝑔; the scale has nothing to push back against and reads zero (the person's real weight 𝑚𝑔 has not changed, but the apparent weight is zero). At the instant of deployment the speed is zero, so the drag is zero and the situation is the same as in (b). Only after the rocket speeds up in its descent does drag grow and the reading rise again.
